analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare drug discount card with out-of-pocket caps for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any action after its two committee referrals, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Medicare beneficiaries voluntarily join a drug discount program run through private companies bidding for contracts, giving them access to negotiated drug prices and an annual fee of $25 that low-income seniors wouldn't pay. It also capped yearly out-of-pocket drug costs: $1,200 for the poorest beneficiaries, $2,500 for those with moderate incomes, and $5,000 for those above that, with the government footing the catastrophic costs. The bill never moved past its committee assignments and expired without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without other drug coverage, especially lower-income seniors. Those under 200% of poverty would pay no enrollment fee and have out-of-pocket drug costs capped at $1,200 a year; moderate-income beneficiaries get a $2,500 cap; all enrollees get access to discounted drug prices negotiated by competing private plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Enrolled beneficiaries would get access to negotiated prices and discounts on prescription drugs through competing private plans, enforced via a uniform discount card issued by the government [S3].
A government-funded catastrophic benefit caps annual out-of-pocket drug spending at $1,200 for beneficiaries below 200% of poverty, $2,500 for those between 200% and 400%, and $5,000 above that [S3].
The $25 annual enrollment fee is waived for beneficiaries with incomes below 200% of the poverty line [S3].
Enrollees get guaranteed issue regardless of health status, appeal rights for formulary denials, and the right of any willing pharmacy in a plan's area to join its network [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The catastrophic benefit and program costs are paid from the Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, with appropriations to cover any excess over the $25 enrollment fees; taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries bear that cost [S3]. Beneficiaries also pay their own drug costs up to the caps.

drawbacks.text: It is not comprehensive drug coverage: the richest protection is a $5,000 annual out-of-pocket cap, and beneficiaries above 600% of poverty get no catastrophic coverage at all, only discounts [S3].

The benefit is delivered entirely through private entities — pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacy delivery systems — that compete on discounts and formularies, with the government paying administrative fees per prescription rather than negotiating drug prices directly [S3].
Discounts apply only to drugs on a plan's formulary, and the catastrophic benefit is means-tested through IRS income data shared with a new Medicare Prescription Drug Agency [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For lower- and middle-income seniors with large drug bills, the catastrophic caps would have been real, immediate relief, and the design protects them from being denied enrollment or losing pharmacy access. But the bill stops well short of a full drug benefit: the well-off get only a modest discount card, everyone remains exposed to the underlying list prices that private middlemen negotiate, and taxpayers fund the catastrophic risk while private entities earn per-prescription fees. It is a help-but-modest design, and in the event its tradeoffs never had to be judged — it died without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their health subcommittees; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Foley (R-FL) introduced the bill on July 25, 2001, joined by Reps. Capito and Terry [S1, S3].
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and in August 2001 to the Health Subcommittee of each [S5].
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on October 5, 2001 — the last recorded action [S5].
The bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No beneficiary gained anything from the bill's death — seniors continued to pay full drug costs through 2003 with no Medicare drug benefit. Nor was any new contract stream created for pharmacy benefit managers or insurers under this design; the status quo continued while Congress debated drug coverage without enacting any version.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply expired

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's entire recorded support was its Republican sponsor and three Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic backing and no opposition ever stated on the record.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill designates private PBMs, insurers, and pharmacy delivery systems as the exclusive contracted channels through which Medicare beneficiaries would get drug discounts and the catastrophic benefit, paying them a negotiated administrative fee per prescription. Beneficiaries would gain coverage, but the public benefit would permanently run through private middlemen rather than direct government provision [S3].

Any pharmacy in a plan's service area may join its network if it accepts the plan's terms, and plans must fund pharmacist-provided medication therapy management programs with fees reflecting the time involved [S3].

The bill sets no government drug prices; discounts come from private negotiation, while the catastrophic subsidy increases the number of prescriptions filled. Drug makers would gain volume without direct price regulation, though plans must encourage generic use [S3].
